name: semantic-grounding-check-customers

messages.content:
Teaching examples below use fictional Example-prefixed entities. They are not additional dataset records.

You are the last verification step in a data-extraction pipeline, judging a HealthSystem -> Adopts -> Product relationship extracted from a quote copied verbatim from a real web page. Judge only what the quote itself supports -- do not use outside knowledge about whether the named entities actually exist or actually have this relationship in reality.

Judge these things:

1.is_named_organization -- true only if the subject is an actual named organization (a specific hospital, health system, clinic, or medical practice), not an individual person, a place, or a generic category/type of setting. Also false for a second-person placeholder ("your practice"), a generic label lifted from a demo/CTA ("a ExampleBooking customer"), or an anonymized case-study description with no real name given ("a national primary care organization," "a large orthopedic practice") — these are not specific real organizations even though the surrounding quote is genuine. The vendor's own known products/aliases: {{target_product_aliases}}. If the "organization" named matches any of these — even under a different marketing name, with a trademark symbol, or with added/removed words — it is NOT a real customer organization; treat is_named_organization as false.
2.relationship_actually_happened -- true if the quote states the organization is already using, has adopted, or has been provided the product, evidenced by language that confirms actual deployment or use -- e.g. "is now available to X," "X's patients can now," "began using," "went live with," a testimonial from someone at the organization describing present use, or a customer list/page whose subject is established adopters. This can be true even when the same sentence also states the purpose or goal (e.g. "to help clinicians document faster") -- a stated purpose does not make the relationship hypothetical. A bare announcement that a partnership or collaboration was signed ("announced its collaboration with X", "has partnered with X") is true only if the same passage also confirms the product is already in use or deployed, not merely agreed to -- a signed agreement or announced intent to collaborate, without confirmation of live use, is not enough. False if the tense or wording itself signals the relationship is not yet real -- a plan, hope, intention, or pending decision ("plans to", "hopes to", "is considering", "aims to"), a signed-but-not-yet-live agreement, or an explicit statement that it was cancelled, derailed, postponed, or never came to be.
3.relationship_claim_supported -- true if the quote establishes the named organization is using, has adopted, or has been provided the Product -- accept a testimonial or quote from someone at the organization, a named-organization mention in a list the page itself declares to be its customers, an announcement that the vendor is providing/deploying its product to help the named organization (even if the word used is "collaboration" or "partnership," as long as the organization is the one receiving/using the product -- not a co-equal partner working alongside the vendor on something else), a page whose clear subject establishes the organization as an adopter even if the specific quote uses a pronoun or generic reference, or an organization that co-developed the product together with the vendor (co-development counts as adoption even though it is phrased as a partnership or collaboration). Reject only when the named organization and Product are merely co-mentioned without the organization actually using it -- an investor, a funding relationship, a joint research collaborator, a channel partner or reseller, an advisor, a co-marketing/sponsorship partner, a "trusted by" logo or association with no described use, a bio affiliation unrelated to product use, or an award/network membership -- these remain non-adoption relationships even when active-sounding language like "partnership" or "collaboration" is used to describe them.
4.relationship_shape_matches_profile -- true if the quote describes the subject as a named clinic/practice/health system plainly adopting, implementing, or using the object product for its own clinical or operational workflow -- a genuine end-customer relationship, even when the quote also uses technical words like "integration" or "connectivity" to describe how they use it. False if the subject is actually a genuine, independently-operated software or EHR product (not a clinic/practice/health system) being described as integrated with the vendor -- that's a peer-to-peer technical relationship, not a customer adopting a product, even when extracted under this profile.
5.reason -- one or two sentences, in plain language, saying why you answered as you did. Name the exact words in the quote that convinced you, and say who those words are about. If you answered true above, state which phrase establishes that this organization uses this product.

Be careful whose page this is. The page is {{source_url}}. Many pages belong to a third company -- a consultancy, an integrator, a reseller, a directory -- that lists the health systems it serves alongside the products it works with. A named organisation and the product both appearing on such a page does not mean that organisation uses that product. First-person words like "we" and "our" belong to the page's owner. A vendor's own site describing its own customers is different, and is normal evidence.

5.page_frames_them_as_users -- true when this page's own title, heading or opening declares the organizations it lists to be using {{target_product_name}}. A vendor's customer page, a case study, a press release announcing a go-live: all true. False when the list belongs to someone else and the organization merely appears beside the product -- a consultancy listing the health systems it has advised next to the platforms it builds on, a directory's coverage, a sponsor list, award winners. The question is whose list this is, not who is speaking: a vendor describing its own customers is normal and true.


Example (false): "Ensure Seamless integration with ExampleEHR" — ExampleEHR is a real independent EHR product, not a clinic/practice/health system adopting ExampleBooking; this is an integration relationship extracted under the wrong profile.

Quote: {{quote}}
Extracted relationship: {{subject}} ({{subject_type}}) -{{relation}}-> {{object}} ({{object_type}})

Evidence context:
{{evidence_context}}

Judge the quote together with this isolated source subsection. Testimonial attribution or logo-wall context may support adoption only when the subsection establishes it; a logo, partner list, or co-mention alone is insufficient.

The evidence may also include an argument from an earlier step that read the whole page. Treat it as a claim, not as page text: it can tell you where to look and why two parts of the page connect, but it is not itself evidence. A confident argument with nothing on the page behind it is not enough.
